title: Methodus generalior numeros quosvis satis grandes perscrutandi utrum sint primi necne?

deep.reconstruction:
Problem served: prove that N = 1000003 is prime. The method is to show that N has only one representation by a binary form αx² + βy² whose product αβ is an idoneal number (numerus idoneus).

Setup (§28, previous page): 1000003 = 3·577² + 19·8². Here α = 3, β = 19 and αβ = 57, which is idoneal. Euler writes x = 7 + 19z and divides by 19, giving 52624 − 42z − 57z² = y². He splits by parity of z:
- z = 2a gives formula A.
- z = 4b + 1 is excluded, because the expression is then ≡ 5 (mod 8).
- z = 4b − 1 gives B = 52609 + 288b − 912b² = y².
A was split further into C and D on the previous pages. Only the known solution turned up there.

This page, §32–33: Euler finishes the search on B. Since y² ≥ 0 forces |b| ≤ 7, he needs b = ±1, …, ±7. Instead of evaluating 912b² ∓ 288b directly, he uses first differences:
- Left column (b > 0): 624, 2448, 4272, …, 11568.
- Right column (b < 0): 1200, 3024, …, 12144.
Both sequences grow by the constant second difference 1824 = 2·912. He subtracts these cumulatively from 52609, in two columns, and checks each remainder for being a square. None is a square.

Conclusion (§33): apart from the known case, 1000003 = 3x² + 19y² has exactly one representation, so it is prime.

§34: the lesson is that larger α and β (with αβ idoneal) shorten the search. Euler then prints his table of the 65 idoneal numbers, 1 through 1848. A number represented in exactly one way by αx² + βy² with αβ in this list is prime.
errors: No arithmetic errors on this page. I checked every cumulative subtraction, e.g. 52609−624=51985, …, 21505−11568=9937 and 18049−12144=5905. None of the remainders is a square (e.g. 39169 lies between 197² and 198²; 28369 between 168² and 169²).

The criterion 'unique representation by αx²+βy² with αβ idoneal ⇒ prime' is stated without the side conditions later made precise by Gauss and Grube. These are: primitivity (gcd(x,y)=1), N coprime to 2αβ, and care with prime powers. In this example the conditions are tacitly satisfied (Euler requires x prime to β and y prime to α in §38), so the conclusion is correct: 1000003 is prime.

Previous page, not this page: in §30 the case giving the square 4 is labelled d = −4. Under the substitution a = 4d − 1 into 3280 + 93d − 228d², it is actually d = +4 (a = 15, z = 30, x = 577). This is a sign-labelling slip only.
The table is offered 'quousque eam continuare licuit' (as far as it could be continued). Euler gives no proof that it is complete.

ideas.what: Primality proof of 1000003 by showing a unique representation by 3x²+19y² (αβ = 57 idoneal), done by exhaustive search organised by congruence splitting
ideas.modern_name: Euler's idoneal-number primality criterion (convenient numbers); one-class-per-genus forms
ideas.usually_credited_to: Euler (idoneal numbers); made rigorous by Gauss (Disquisitiones, genus theory) and Grube (1874)
ideas.where_published: E708, E715, E719, E725 and related papers in Nova Acta / Opera postuma; discussed in Weil, 'Number Theory: An Approach through History'

ideas.what: Evaluating a quadratic at successive integers by subtracting first differences that increase by a constant second difference (1824)
ideas.modern_name: Method of finite differences for tabulating polynomials
Idoneal numbers (n for which each genus of forms of discriminant −4n has one class)
ideas.usually_credited_to: Euler; completeness up to at most one further number proved by Weinberger (1973); complete under GRH
ideas.where_published: E708 ('De variis modis numeros praegrandes examinandi…') and E725, among others

deep.surprise_reason: This is a well-known worked example of Euler's idoneal-number primality test, plus his standard 65-entry table. All of it is documented in the literature (Weil, Grube, Weinberger). The page has no new result, unfinished thread, or unnoticed connection.
transcription_corrections: §33 conclusion: the image reads '3xx + 19yy' (α = 3, β = 19), not '3xx + 199yy'.
Page 22's text continues mid-sentence onto page 23 ('…in duabus columnis…' then 'ubi nullum plane quadratum occurrit'); the catchword 'ubi' at the foot of p. 22 is correctly reproduced.
